title: History of the Bhang-Eater and His Wife

keywords: history of the bhang-eater and his wife
full_text:
In the town of Homs lived an amiable but foolish man named Salim, who wasted his meager earnings on sweet herbal confections that filled his head with absurd fantasies.
His prudent and devoted wife, Zubayda, despaired of his indolence, for their cupboards were often bare while Salim sat on the roof smiling at invisible angels.

One evening, Salim returned home with a glaze in his eyes, sat upon the floor, and declared:
'Zubayda, rejoice! I have just been appointed Supreme Admiral of the Red Sea Fleet! Tomorrow morning, thirty war galleys with purple sails will dock in our garden pond to await my commands!'

Zubayda looked at the tiny stone pond in their courtyard, which barely held three ducks, and decided it was time to cure her husband once and for all.

She set an empty clay bowl before him and an empty wooden spoon, saying:
'O Great Admiral, feast upon this royal banquet of roasted pheasants stuffed with almonds and saffron rice!'

Salim stared at the empty bowl: 'Wife, the bowl is completely empty!'
Zubayda feigned astonishment: 'What? Can an Admiral who sees thirty war galleys in a duck pond not see roasted pheasants in a porcelain bowl? Eat, my lord, eat of the feast thy imagination has prepared!'

Salim blinked, realizing the biting absurdity of his pretensions.
Next, Zubayda brought him an empty pottery jug: 'Drink, my Admiral, this goblet of cooled pomegranate sherbet!'
Salim tilted the dry jug to his lips, but nothing came out.

He sat back, his stomach growling loudly in the quiet room.
'Zubayda,' he admitted softly, 'I am terribly hungry, and empty air cannot fill my belly.'

Zubayda then brought from the kitchen a warm, fragrant dish of real lentil stew, freshly baked flatbread, and a wedge of white cheese.
'Here is real food, Salim, purchased with real coins earned by real spinning. If thou wilt be an honest weaver instead of an imaginary admiral, thy home will never lack bread, warmth, or honor.'

Salim wept, embraced his wise wife, and swore to touch foolish stimulants no more. He returned to his loom the next dawn, worked with diligence, and within a year owned a thriving textile shop, blessed by the love and wisdom of his faithful wife.
moral: Patience and clever household management can guide a straying spouse back to reason and domestic harmony.
